articleSummary: An outbreak of invasive meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) has been reported in a school in Ho Chi Minh City. articleSummary: Outbreak of meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) linked to a school in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, underscores why this low-incidence infection can trigger red alerts. The core driver is asymptomatic carriage: about 5-10% of the population (up to 20-25% among adolescents) harbor meningococcus in the throat and transmit via respiratory droplets, especially in crowded, poorly ventilated settings. A single case can spark rapid spread in schools and other dense environments. Meningococcal disease can progress from fever or sore throat to septicemia and meningitis within 24 hours, with a case-fatality of 10-15% despite ICU treatment, and 10-20% of survivors sustaining lifelong sequelae such as limb loss, deafness, brain injury, epilepsy, or chronic kidney impairment. Vaccination gaps against five serogroups (A, B, C, W-135, Y) leave communities vulnerable. Prevention priorities: broad vaccination, improved ventilation, hand hygiene, avoiding shared utensils, and prompt outbreak containment, especially before entry to schools or dormitories.

articleSummary: DR Congo is testing a new Ebola vaccine as part of intensified containment efforts to curb transmission, amid expectations about its safety and efficacy from ongoing trials. The study aims to evaluate immune responses, monitor potential adverse effects, and identify groups likely to benefit during the trial phases. Initiating vaccine testing does not imply immediate readiness for general use; deployment depends on clinical trial outcomes demonstrating safety and efficacy to medical standards. Concurrently, health authorities continue outbreak response through infection surveillance, isolation of confirmed cases, contact tracing, and risk communication, while ensuring protection for frontline workers. The Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an Ebola outbreak in mid-May, a highly dangerous disease that has caused more than 15,000 deaths in Africa over the past five decades.

articleHeadline: Adenovirus gây tổn thương đồng thời đường hô hấp, mắt
articleSummary: Adenovirus infection with simultaneous respiratory and ocular involvement diagnosed in a 35-year-old woman in Hanoi, Vietnam. Rapid testing at MEDLATEC was negative for influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, and Dengue NS1; Adenovirus antigen was positive. Diagnosed with acute purulent pharyngitis and acute bilateral conjunctivitis. Blood tests showed inflammatory markers: WBC 9.07 x10^9/L (normal), monocytes 10.6%, CRP 29.61 mg/L. Transmission occurs via close contact, respiratory droplets, and contaminated surfaces; conjunctivitis spreads through eye discharge and shared items. Treatment: outpatient, symptomatic care; antibiotics used only if bacterial coinfection suspected. Most healthy adults recover with supportive care, though pneumonia and other complications can occur in high-risk groups.

articleSummary: Newcastle disease found on a second Brazilian poultry farm in Coronel Freitas, Santa Catarina, a week after the first case at Nova Itaberaba (both turkey units). articleSummary: Malaria kills about 600,000 people annually, mostly African children under five, per the WHO. Columbia University researchers in New York have captured in action the mobile junction, the ring-like gateway the parasite uses to invade red blood cells. Using cryo-electron microscopy, they froze samples to preserve proteins and recorded the exact moment of entry: the junction opens a brief pore in the red blood cell membrane and then seals it as molecular clamps assemble and the cell surface is remodeled. The mobile junction is the entry route for all human-infecting Plasmodium species, making it an attractive drug target. Blocking it could stop blood-stage replication and guide therapies for related parasites causing cyclosporiasis and toxoplasmosis. In Brazil’s Amazon, malaria remains high (100k+ cases annually, mainly Plasmodium vivax); vaccines RTS,S and R21 offer partial protection, and artemisinin resistance is spreading in parts of Africa and Asia. articleSummary: Oral fluralaner (Bravecto) achieved 100% wound clearance in dogs with natural New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) infestations in endemic regions of Brazil, according to a multicenter Parasites & Vectors study. articleSummary: As of 26 October 2026, researchers from China, Australia, and Singapore link marine virus CMNV to an emergent human eye disease labeled POH-VAU. In a study of 70 patients, the disease’s anterior segment causes recurrent inflammation and chronically elevated intraocular pressure, risking optic nerve damage and vision loss. Laboratory analyses detected CMNV in ocular tissues and immune markers indicating prior infection, supporting a virus-eye disease connection. The study highlights a marine-origin spillover from aquatic animals to humans, with the most common exposure routes being direct handling of fish and shellfish during cleaning/preparation and consumption of undercooked or raw seafood; together these factors accounted for about 71.4% of cases. Preventive measures include gloves, thorough handwashing, avoiding raw seafood, and prompt ophthalmologic evaluation for redness, pain, blurred vision, or recurrent inflammation.

articleSummary: As of 26 October 2026, six houseplants—pothos (jiboia), lucky bamboo, peace lily (lírio-da-paz), variegata, Monstera deliciosa (costela-de-adão), and 'swords and spears'—can be grown in water with roots exposed. For pothos, use a cut with at least one node and keep the node in contact with water while leaves remain above. Monstera deliciosa can propagate from a node cut with a leaf outside. articleHeadline: PGK1 kinase activity disables a host chaperone to restrict multiple viruses
articleSummary: PGK1, a glycolytic enzyme, acts as a non-canonical protein kinase to restrict replication of multiple viruses by targeting the host chaperone HSP90AA1. This host-directed antiviral mechanism operates independently of PGK1’s glycolytic function and may reflect a broader defense strategy. Influenza A nucleoprotein can compete with HSP90AA1 for PGK1, suggesting a viral immune evasion tactic. articleSummary: As of 27 October 2026, Kulon Progo District Health Office in Indonesia records 64 leptospirosis cases and 7 deaths in 2026. Most affected are workers in wet environments, notably farmers and day laborers. Prompt antibiotic treatment is urged to avert renal and hepatic complications and death. PHBS (Clean and Healthy Living) and environmental sanitation are emphasized to reduce exposure, especially in areas with standing water, water storage, and wells. Leptospira bacteria are shed in rat urine and contaminate water bodies such as flooded rice paddies. Historical data show annual leptospirosis fatalities since 2012, peaking in 2023 with 12 deaths; a reduction occurred in 2021 (11 cases, 1 death).

articleHeadline: Caso de zika vírus é confirmado em viajante russa após retorno de temporada na Indonésia
articleSummary: Laboratory-confirmed Zika virus infection in a Russian traveler who spent two weeks in Bali, Indonesia, and was hospitalized after returning to Russia. The patient developed fever of 38°C, chills and a mild rash, and recovered following hospital treatment, being discharged without complications. Russia does not have endemic Zika transmission; all reported cases are imported, linked to travel to endemic areas such as Indonesia. Zika is primarily transmitted by mosquitoes in tropical regions, and there is no vaccine or specific antiviral therapy. Prevention for travelers focuses on vector exposure reduction: proven insect repellents, long-sleeved clothing and lightweight trousers, and the use of bed nets, especially when lodging lacks air conditioning or tightly sealed windows. As of 26 October 2026, the case highlights ongoing importation risk from Southeast Asia.

articleSummary: As of 26 October 2026, a Swiss national treated for Ebola in Nigeria has been evacuated to Switzerland with her husband for medical reasons. Nigeria says she is the first confirmed case in the current outbreak there; she left Abuja early Monday with consent and remains stable, communicative, and under strict containment, as she may still be contagious. Her husband, a Swiss diplomat, is asymptomatic and isolated in Zurich. The couple arrived on a medical-evacuation flight; she is hospitalized at Geneva University Hospitals and he is in isolation at Zurich University Hospital. Nigeria continues to monitor 52 contacts and, at present, has no active Ebola cases. The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda; authorities have not yet determined how she contracted it. The outbreak centers on Bundibugyo virus with spread beyond DRC; Kenya reports 9 cases, 2 deaths; DRC totals exceed 9,900 cases and 4,800 deaths; initial cases in Nigeria and Kenya traced to Entebbe, Uganda.
